newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow "surprised" by U.S. stand on missiles.
newsitem.headline: Moscow "surprised" by U.S. stand on missiles.

text.p: Russia expressed "surprise and regret" on Thursday at the collapse of an agreement with the United States on regional missile defences, clearly implying that Washington was to blame.

The agreement was to have been signed at a ceremony in Geneva on Thursday, but the State Department announced on Wednesday that the deal was off, at least for now, and suggested Russia had changed its position.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Mikhail Demurin said on Thursday Russia was ready to sign the missile deal documents "if they are properly prepared."

Demurin, quoted by Itar-Tass news agency, appeared to confirm that Moscow was insisting on progress towards a second-stage missile pact before signing up for the first-stage deal that was on the table in Geneva.

"Our starting point is that the deputy foreign ministers must review the progress reached in work on the second stage of limitations," Demurin said, adding that Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Mamedov had flown to Geneva with this in view.

The agreement announced by U.S Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov last month would specify which short-range defence missile systems are allowed under the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty.

Deploying regional defences against missiles has become increasingly popular in the United States but Russia is adamant that theatre missile defences should not undermine the Soviet-American ABM treaty.

The ABM pact, considered by many experts a cornerstone of international arms control, limits defences against strategic -- or long-range -- missiles but was not meant to address regional missile defences.
But the United States and Russia had been negotiating what systems could be pursued legally under the treaty.

At their September meeting in New York, Christopher and Primakov agreed to permit deployment of lower-speed theatre missile defence systems of up to two miles (3 km) per second provided they are not tested against faster, longer-range ballistic missile targets.
Russia wants to see progress on a more controversial second-phase pact governing faster systems, which is also under negotiation.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns on Wednesday pointed the finger at Primakov, saying: "The Russian foreign minister made a very specific agreement with Secretary of State Christopher. We expect that should be honoured."
